title: Drilling لَمْ and لَمَّا — Three Ways to Say Not Yet, and Why You Reason from the Rule
summary: A session of applied practice on the two past-tense negations, opening with a methodological correction that shapes the whole class: a student reads هَارُونَ because that is how it sounds in the Qur'ān, and the teacher presses him to work from the rule instead — here هَارُون is the فَاعِل, so it must be هَارُونُ. The same principle settles سَأَلَكَ against سَأَلْتَ, where the ending alone decides who is asking whom. The lesson also gives three equivalent ways to say not yet, and the difference between the formal لَمَّا and the colloquial لِسَّه.
key_points: The method that matters more than any single rule: do not read by what sounds right. A form may sound familiar because of how it appears in one Qur'ānic context, while the sentence in front of you calls for something else. Here هَارُون is the doer of ذَهَبَ, so it takes a ḍamma — هَارُونُ.

Endings carry meaning, not just correctness. سَأَلَكَ الْمُدِيرُ means the principal asked you — the attached كَ is the مَفْعُول and الْمُدِير the فَاعِل — whereas سَأَلْتَ الْمُدِيرَ would mean you asked the principal. Misreading the ending reverses the sentence.
Three equivalent ways to say something has not happened yet: لَمَّا أَكْتُبْ, لَمْ أَكْتُبْ بَعْدُ, and مَا كَتَبْتُ إِلَى الْآنَ. بَعْدُ and إِلَى الْآنَ both supply the sense of yet.
لَمَّا can even stand alone as a complete answer. Asked أَرَجَعَ أَبُوكَ, one may reply simply لَمَّا — not yet — without repeating the verb.
لَمْ requires the مُضَارِع form, so an answer must convert the past tense of the question: to أَكَتَبْتُمُ الْوَاجِبَ one answers لَمَّا نَكْتُبِ الْوَاجِبَاتِ, not كَتَبْنَا.
When answering the book's questions you take on the persona of whoever is addressed: a question put to Zaynab is answered as Zaynab, and one put to a mother is answered as the mother.
The hamza of أَكَتَبْتُمْ is هَمْزَة الِاسْتِفْهَام and not part of the verb — أَقَرَأْنَا is the question did we read, so the answer uses نَقْرَأْ.
لِسَّه is the colloquial word Arabs commonly use for not yet, but it is عَامِّيَّة. The book's author instructs teachers to steer students to لَمَّا, the form used in proper Arabic and in the Qur'ān.

Much عَامِّيَّة traces back to فُصْحَى once you look: إِيش comes from أَيُّ شَيْءٍ (what thing), and وَيْنَك from أَيْنَ أَنْتَ. Dialects then distort the sounds — in Egypt a qāf is pronounced as a hamza, so الْمُقَطَّم becomes al-Muʾaṭṭam, and a jīm becomes a hard g.
جَمْع مُؤَنَّث سَالِم keeps taking a kasra where a fatḥa would be due: الْوَاجِبَاتِ.
رَئِيس means president or leader, from رَأْس (head), and اِسْتِقْبَال is receiving or welcoming, as in Urdu.
Vocabulary: بَقَّال (grocer or shopkeeper), دِمَشْق (Damascus), الطَّائِف (Taif), قَمِيص with its plural قُمْصَان, نَظَّارَة (eyeglasses), الْبَارِحَة (last night), and سَمَحَ (to give permission).

The teacher's study advice: watch for لَمْ every time you read the Qur'ān and check the verb after it. Noticing the pattern repeatedly is what turns a rule into second nature — reading without attending to the grammar will not do it.
questions: [00:00:00] Q: Why isn't it هَارُونَ, since that is how it sounds in the Qur'ān? — A: Because there it occurs in a context that calls for a fatḥa. Here هَارُون is the فَاعِل of ذَهَبَ, so it takes a ḍamma. Work from the rule, not from what sounds familiar.
[00:02:00] Q: What does رَئِيس mean? — A: President or leader — رَأْس is head, and رَئِيس is built from it.
[00:02:00] Q: What is اِسْتِقْبَال? — A: To receive or welcome, the same as in Urdu.
[00:08:02] Q: Does سَمَحَ mean to permit? — A: Yes, to give permission — لَمْ يَسْمَحْ لِي بِالْخُرُوجِ, he did not allow me to go out.
[00:13:00] Q: I answered as though speaking about Hārūn rather than as him. — A: The question asks did you break it, so you answer as Hārūn. To say he did not break it you would use a different form.

[00:17:00] Q: If I made the كَ the doer instead, what would change? — A: The meaning would reverse. أَسَأَلَكَ الْمُدِيرُ is the principal asked you; to say you asked him it must be أَسَأَلْتَ الْمُدِيرَ. Whenever a كَ follows a verb you can expect it to be the object.
[00:20:00] Q: What does بَعْدُ mean here? — A: Yet. لَمْ أَكْتُبْ بَعْدُ and مَا كَتَبْتُ إِلَى الْآنَ both say the same as لَمَّا أَكْتُبْ.
[00:24:00] Q: What is wrong with answering كَتَبْنَا? — A: لَمَّا needs a مُضَارِع verb, so it must be لَمَّا نَكْتُبْ.
[00:24:00] Q: Why is it الْوَاجِبَاتِ with a kasra? — A: Because it is جَمْع مُؤَنَّث سَالِم, which substitutes a kasra for the accusative fatḥa.
[00:32:00] Q: Would Arabs understand لَمَّا if we used it instead of لِسَّه? — A: Yes. Even those who speak only عَامِّيَّة day to day will understand it if they have been through school.

quiz.q: In ذَهَبَ هَارُونُ, why does هَارُون take a ḍamma?
options: Because it is a proper noun
Because it is the فَاعِل of the verb
quiz.a: The teacher's point about method: the doer is مَرْفُوع, regardless of how the name sounds in a familiar Qur'ānic phrase.

options: Did you ask about the principal?
Did the principal ask about you?
quiz.a: The attached كَ is the object and الْمُدِير the doer, so the principal is the one asking.

quiz.q: Which three expressions all mean I have not written yet?
options: لَمْ أَكْتُبْ، لَنْ أَكْتُبَ، مَا أَكْتُبُ
لَمَّا أَكْتُبْ، لَمْ أَكْتُبْ بَعْدُ، مَا كَتَبْتُ إِلَى الْآنَ
لَا أَكْتُبُ، لَمْ أَكْتُبْ، لَنْ أَكْتُبَ
مَا كَتَبْتُ، لَا أَكْتُبُ، لَنْ أَكْتُبَ
quiz.a: The book gives these three as equivalents, with بَعْدُ and إِلَى الْآنَ both supplying the sense of yet.

quiz.q: Can لَمَّا be used as a complete answer on its own?
options: No, it always needs a verb
Yes — لَمَّا alone conveys not yet
quiz.a: To أَرَجَعَ أَبُوكَ one can simply answer لَمَّا, and it will be understood.

quiz.q: What is wrong with answering أَكَتَبْتُمُ الْوَاجِبَ with لَمَّا كَتَبْنَا?
options: لَمَّا requires a مُضَارِع verb, so it must be لَمَّا نَكْتُبْ
لَمَّا cannot be used in answers
quiz.a: Both لَمْ and لَمَّا take the مُضَارِع form, even though the meaning is past.

quiz.q: In أَقَرَأْنَا, what is the role of the opening hamza?
options: It is part of the verb
It is هَمْزَة الِاسْتِفْهَام, marking a question
It makes the verb first person
quiz.a: The verb is قَرَأْنَا, we read; the hamza turns it into did we read.

quiz.q: What is لِسَّه, and why does the book discourage it?
options: A formal word that is simply rare
The colloquial word for not yet; the book directs students to the proper لَمَّا
quiz.a: It is عَامِّيَّة. The author instructs teachers to have students use لَمَّا instead.

quiz.q: What is إِيش in colloquial Arabic derived from?
quiz.a: أَيُّ شَيْءٍ — which thing — compressed into إِيش, just as أَيْنَ أَنْتَ becomes وَيْنَك.
From رَأْس, head — hence the leader or president.

quiz.q: What is the plural of قَمِيص?
quiz.a: قُمْصَان — so قُمْصَانَك is your shirts, in the exercise about washing them.

quran_examples.translation: Did We not expand for you your breast?
quran_examples.note: A clear instance of لَمْ: نَشْرَحُ becomes نَشْرَحْ with the sukūn while the meaning is past. The verb شَرَحَ is also the lesson's own vocabulary item for explaining.

quran_examples.arabic: أَلَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصْحَابِ الْفِيلِ
quran_examples.transliteration: a-lam tara kayfa faʿala rabbuka bi-aṣḥābi al-fīl
quran_examples.translation: Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?
quran_examples.note: Shows the irregular تَرَى losing its final letter when لَمْ puts it in jazm — تَرَ — the same behaviour the class had seen with لَمْ يَأْتِ.

quran_examples.arabic: هَلْ أَتَىٰ عَلَى الْإِنسَانِ حِينٌ مِّنَ الدَّهْرِ لَمْ يَكُن شَيْئًا مَّذْكُورًا
quran_examples.transliteration: hal atā ʿalā al-insāni ḥīnun mina al-dahri lam yakun shayʾan madhkūrā
quran_examples.translation: Has there not come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing mentioned?
quran_examples.note: كَانَ، يَكُونُ becomes يَكُنْ in jazm after لَمْ, with the meaning firmly in the past.

quran_examples.arabic: أَمْ حَسِبْتُمْ أَن تَدْخُلُوا الْجَنَّةَ وَلَمَّا يَأْتِكُم مَّثَلُ الَّذِينَ خَلَوْا مِن قَبْلِكُمْ
quran_examples.transliteration: am ḥasibtum an tadkhulū al-jannata wa-lammā yaʾtikum mathalu alladhīna khalaw min qablikum
quran_examples.translation: Or do you think you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the like of what came to those before you?
quran_examples.note: The Qur'ānic لَمَّا with precisely the not yet sense taught here. The āyah also carries أَمْ for the alternative question and أَنْ dropping the نُون from تَدْخُلُونَ.
